newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Fighting intensifies north of Kabul.
newsitem.headline: Fighting intensifies north of Kabul.

text.p: Heavy fighting erupted on the front lines north of the Afghan capital Kabul on Sunday morning, with the Islamic Taleban army claiming to have gained territory.
"We started our attack at 3 a.m. this morning, we have moved up the road and our forces have also attacked from the west and are close to Mir Batcha Kot (17 miles (27 km) north of Kabul).
"There is a small pocket of opposition surrounded and they are still shooting at the road," a Taleban front line commander said.
He said the front line held by opposition forces loyal to former government military chief Ahmad Shah Masood had been broken, but that skirmishing was continuing.
One local resident said that "last night was the heaviest fighting I can remember in the last month".

The young man was being pushed along the road to Kabul in a wheelchair by his younger brothers from the Taleban-held village of Shakar Dara, some 16 miles (25 km) north of Kabul and near the front line.
"It was raining rockets in Shakar Dara so I am going to spend two or three days in Kabul with my relatives." he said.

The Taleban, who captured Kabul in September and control at least two-thirds of Afghanistan, took away at least five dead bodies from the battle zone near Mir Batcha Kot. The bodies were loaded into the back of pick-ups and covered with blankets.

Heavy exchanges of artillery and rocket fire were continuing, and opposition jets bombed Taleban positions close to the front line sending those nearby scurrying for cover. There were no immediate reports of casualties from the bombing.
The Taleban were using helicopter gunships against opposition positions. They wheeled low over the front line before launching their rockets to explode in clouds of dust.

Three weeks ago the opposition forces commanded by Masood, a veteran of almost 20 years of conflict in Afghanistan, broke out of their stronghold in the foothills of the Hindu Kush mountains to push towards Kabul.
The opposition control a salient of territory running south along a valley leading from the mountains towards Kabul.
Despite daily artillery and rocket duels and sporadic attacks from both sides, there has been little movement since the opposition advance.
The Taleban want to impose their strict Islamic rule throughout the country, but have failed to quell opposition from various northern ethnic minorities.
